newsitem.title: UK: You can trust me, down-to-earth Major tells Britain.
newsitem.headline: You can trust me, down-to-earth Major tells Britain.

text.p: John Major on Friday put his reputation as a trustworthy man of the people at the heart of the ruling Conservative party's campaign to win a fifth straight term of office at Britain's coming election.

Throughout an understated closing address to the Conservatives' annual conference, the prime minister contrasted his practical experience with the untested ambitions of a Labour party oppostion he attacked as elitist and opportunist.
"At this election there's a central question. It's this: who can be trusted with the future?" the prime minster asked.

Major, exuding quiet confidence after a week in which pro- and anti-European factions agreed to bury the hatchet for the sake of party unity, hammered home the need for harmony in the run-up to the general election, due by May.

"The lesson is clear. Everyone in the Conservative party should work - and if I know them, will work -- heart and soul, irrespective of personal interests, to secure the re-election of a Conservative government," he said.
Labour, in opposition since 1979, led the Conservatives by around 20 percentage points in opinion polls before this week.
But Major's speech gave supporters the chance to dream the impossible dream -- that just like the last election they could defy opinion polls and return the Conservatives to power again.

Bookmakers were expecting a narrowing of the odds against a Conservative victory after a conference that went better than party managers had dared to imagine after months of squabbling over Europe and allegations of sleaze.
"It's been the week the Tory family came together - to renew the family contract with the British nation," Major said.
If his speech was something of an anti-climax, it confirmed Major as the Conservatives' main weapon in the coming battle.
The prime minister consistently scores higher in opinion polls than his party, which voters see as tired and short of ideas after 17-1/2 years in power.

After drawing enthusiastic reviews for a question-and-answer session he conducted in his shirtsleeves on Wednesday, Major said he would also fight the election on meet-the-people lines -- as he did to good effect from a soapbox at the 1992 ballot.
"I'll be where you are," he told his activists. "I'll be the one talking to the people in the middle of the crowd. So come and join me, and I promise you, we'll win."

The simple message sincerely delivered was meant to contrast with the "covenant for the British people" that Labour leader Tony Blair announced last week with what some media critics called an almost messianic intensity.

In an audacious attempt to reverse the traditional roles of the main parties, Major said the Conservatives stood for extending opportunties for "millions of quiet, decent home-loving families up and down our country".
Labour, by contrast, had been capturd by an aloof, comfortably-off elite who wanted the best for themselves but would deny it to others.
Major scored points by comparing his grammar school education with Blair's elitist private-school upbringing. "New Labour, old school tie," he said cuttingly.
And whereas "young" Blair now lived in the fashionable north London district of Islington, Major had taken hard knocks growing up in one of the capital's run-down inner cities.
"I didn't come from two rooms in Brixton to 10, Downing Street not to go out and fight with every fibre of my being for the things I believe in, and the country I love," Major said.
He spelled out how the Conservatives would enhance "opportunity for all" by cutting taxes and reforming welfare to create "a self-help society -- not a help yourself society".
He recapped a raft of initiatives outlined by his ministers, pledged to keep spending more on health and unveiled plans for the electronic tagging of young troublemakers.
In powerful language on Northern Ireland, he condemned the Irish Republican Army for a bomb attack on Monday on Britain's main army base in the province, which killed one soldier.

His voice trembling with emotion, Major paid tribute to the dead man and said no one would take Sinn Fein, the political wing of the IRA, seriously until they showed a serious commitment to end violence for good.

"I promise the people of Northern Ireland this: for as long as there is a political breath in my body,I will fight for a secure way of life in Northern Ireland and for a settlement fair to all," he said.
